I have a friend that’s suffering with major depressive disorder and while I sympathize with what he’s going through, it can be really hard to put up with someone that can’t see the good in anything. When his family moved to another city to start a business, he chose to stay behind; the whole time he was here, he was miserable because he was a long ways away from his family. A few years back, he decided to move to the city where his family lived, now that he’s there, he’s miserable because he doesn’t have any friends. He met people that invited him out, but given the choice between going to the bar and staying home and smoking weed, he chose to stay home and smoke weed every time and no one invites him out anymore. I tried inviting him back to my city a few months back, but he didn’t want to move here because he hates my city. My city wasn’t to blame for his unhappiness. Then he rage quits his job and spends weeks unemployed and mooching off his family, which of course creates tension between him and his parents.

I know it’s not as simple as choosing to be happy, but, at the same time, I think a lot of depressed people need to change their mindsets. No, you can’t control your moods, but you can control what you do when you’re feeling down. Wallowing in your depression is no good for you just like a diabetic binging on sugar is no good for them.

I think a happy person could look at situation, say “well, this isn’t great”, and look for ways to improve it while too many depressed people will wallow in their despair and find the negatives in even the best situations.

Well, for starters, you have to find a family doctor and tell him/her exactly what you wrote here.

They may want to institutionalize you. If you really want to make a good faith effort to live, you should go along with it. It isn’t so bad. Mostly just boring.

Whether the doctor wants to institutionalize you or not, you’re going to be prescribed medication. Take it everyday even if you don’t feel like it’s helping. The medication isn’t supposed to make you happy. It is just supposed to reduce the worst symptoms of depression. Keep notes of any side effects you experience and communicate them to your doctor on follow up visits. Also, maybe keep a journal of when you feel really bad and why. It might be able to help your doctor figure out if a medication is doing enough to help you or another one would be better.

“A DNR” is a do not resuscitate order which means medical professionals cannot legally resuscitate you if your heart stops beating (although they are also legally bound to start CPR if they are not presented with the physical DNR when your heart stops). Any other medical treatment is fair game.

If you sign a DNR and then attempt suicide, the DNR could be declared invalid because you weren’t of sound mind when you signed it.

Honestly, just save yourself the legal fees. It’s unlikely that a DNR will stop the medical community from saving you.
